title: Isaiah Chapter 36 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Isaiah chapter 36 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Isaiah Chapter 36 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Isaiah Chapter 36.

questions.question: In Isaiah 36, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against the cities of Judah
Rabshakeh spoke to Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah
Rabshakeh offered to give two thousand horses
Hezekiah took away high places and altars
questions.correctAnswer: Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against the cities of Judah
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:1 states that Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against the defenced cities of Judah first in the narrative.

questions.question: In which year of King Hezekiah did Sennacherib come up against Judah's cities?
options: Tenth year
Fourteenth year
Twentieth year
First year
questions.correctAnswer: Fourteenth year
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:1 specifies it was in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah that Sennacherib came up.

questions.question: Who did the king of Assyria send from Lachish to Jerusalem?
options: Rabshakeh
Eliakim
Shebna
Joah
questions.correctAnswer: Rabshakeh
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:2 says the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem.

questions.question: Where did Rabshakeh stand when he came to Jerusalem?
options: By the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field
At the city gate
On the temple mount
Near the king's palace
questions.correctAnswer: By the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:2 describes Rabshakeh standing by the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field.

questions.question: Who came forth to meet Rabshakeh?
options: Eliakim, Hilkiah's son, Shebna the scribe, and Joah, Asaph's son
King Hezekiah himself
The priests of the temple
The elders of Jerusalem
questions.correctAnswer: Eliakim, Hilkiah's son, Shebna the scribe, and Joah, Asaph's son
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:3 states that Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah came to Rabshakeh.

questions.question: What question did Rabshakeh ask concerning Hezekiah's confidence?
options: What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?
Why do you build walls around the city?
Where is your army stationed?
Who is your God?
questions.correctAnswer: What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:4 records Rabshakeh asking, "What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?"

questions.question: According to Rabshakeh, what is Hezekiah's counsel and strength for?
options: War
Peace
Trade
Building
questions.correctAnswer: War
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:5 says Hezekiah claims to have counsel and strength for war.

questions.question: On what does Rabshakeh say Hezekiah is trusting as a 'broken reed'?
options: Egypt
Babylon
Assyria
Moab
questions.correctAnswer: Egypt
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:6 states that Hezekiah trusts on Egypt, called a broken reed.

questions.question: What will happen if a man leans on the 'staff of this broken reed' according to Rabshakeh?
options: It will go into his hand and pierce it
It will break and fall
It will grow stronger
It will support him firmly
questions.correctAnswer: It will go into his hand and pierce it
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:6 describes that if a man leans on the broken reed, it will go into his hand and pierce it.

questions.question: What had Hezekiah taken away that related to the LORD God, according to Rabshakeh?
options: High places and altars
Walls of the city
The king's horses
The army's weapons
questions.correctAnswer: High places and altars
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:7 says Hezekiah took away the high places and altars of the LORD God.

questions.question: What did Rabshakeh offer to give if riders could be set upon horses?
options: Two thousand horses
Five hundred chariots
A thousand soldiers
Three thousand camels
questions.correctAnswer: Two thousand horses
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:8 shows Rabshakeh offering two thousand horses if riders could be set upon them.

questions.question: Rabshakeh came to Jerusalem with a great army, sent by the king of Assyria.
options: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:2 states the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh with a great army to Jerusalem.

questions.question: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah were officials who went out to meet Rabshakeh.
options: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:3 identifies Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah as those who came out to Rabshakeh.

questions.question: Rabshakeh threatened to destroy Jerusalem with a flood of water.
options: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: The text in Isaiah 36:1-8 does not mention Rabshakeh threatening Jerusalem with a flood of water.

questions.question: Hezekiah trusted in the strength of his chariots and horses to defend Jerusalem.
options: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:1-8 does not say Hezekiah trusted in chariots and horses; instead, Rabshakeh mocks trust in Egypt and God.

medium.title: Isaiah Chapter 36 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Isaiah Chapter 36 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What does Rabshakeh mockingly suggest the men on the wall will have to eat and drink?
options: Their own dung and piss
Bread and water
The fruits of the land
Meat and wine
questions.correctAnswer: Their own dung and piss
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh said they would eat their own dung and drink their own piss as a form of humiliation and desperation (Isaiah 36:12).

questions.question: What does Isaiah 36:15 promise will happen if people trust in the LORD as Hezekiah advises?
options: The city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria
The king of Assyria will conquer the city
Hezekiah will be captured
The people will suffer famine
questions.correctAnswer: The city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:15 explains that trusting in the LORD will result in the city not being delivered into Assyria's hand.

questions.question: What reason does Rabshakeh give to reject trusting in Egypt for help?
options: Egypt is like a broken reed that pierces the hand
Egypt has no chariots or horsemen
Egypt is too far away to help
Egypt is friendly to Assyria
questions.correctAnswer: Egypt is like a broken reed that pierces the hand
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh compares trusting Egypt to leaning on a broken reed that pierces the hand, meaning it is unreliable and harmful (Isaiah 36:9).

questions.question: How does Isaiah 36:14 relate to Isaiah 36:15 in Rabshakeh's speech?
options: Both verses warn against trusting Hezekiah and the LORD to deliver the city
Isaiah 36:14 promises peace, and 36:15 warns of war
Isaiah 36:14 encourages trust, and 36:15 discourages it
Isaiah 36:14 discusses Egypt, and 36:15 discusses Assyria
questions.correctAnswer: Both verses warn against trusting Hezekiah and the LORD to deliver the city
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:14 and 36:15 both contain Rabshakeh's warnings that Hezekiah will not deliver the city and that trusting the LORD will not save them.

questions.question: Why does Rabshakeh say he has come up against the land?
options: Because the LORD commanded him to destroy it
To make peace with Hezekiah
To form an alliance with Judah
To help defend the city
questions.correctAnswer: Because the LORD commanded him to destroy it
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh claims he came up against the land because the LORD told him to go up and destroy it (Isaiah 36:10).

questions.question: What does Rabshakeh command the people to do if they make an agreement with the king of Assyria?
options: Eat every one of his vine and fig tree and drink the waters of his cistern
Flee to Egypt for safety
Prepare to fight to the death
Build altars to the LORD
questions.correctAnswer: Eat every one of his vine and fig tree and drink the waters of his cistern
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:16 records Rabshakeh instructing them to accept the king's terms and enjoy his provisions.

questions.question: What is the practical lesson about trusting human strength versus divine help evident in Rabshakeh's speech?
options: Trusting in human allies like Egypt can be unreliable and harmful
Human strength always guarantees victory
Ignoring earthly help and only praying is sufficient
Military power is the only way to survive
questions.correctAnswer: Trusting in human allies like Egypt can be unreliable and harmful
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh mocks trust in Egypt as a broken reed that will pierce the hand, illustrating the danger of relying on human strength over God (Isaiah 36:9).

questions.question: How does Rabshakeh's use of the Jewish language in verse 13 demonstrate a strategy in communication?
options: To intimidate and spread fear directly to the people on the wall
To confuse the officials
To show respect to the leaders
To secretly communicate with his own troops
questions.correctAnswer: To intimidate and spread fear directly to the people on the wall
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh spoke loudly in the Jewish language to ensure all, including the people on the wall, heard his threats and were intimidated (Isaiah 36:13).

questions.question: What practical Christian living principle can be derived from Hezekiah's officials asking Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language?
options: Maintaining integrity by not allowing harmful words to influence the people
Avoiding communication with enemies
Using secret languages for safety
Ignoring threats from adversaries
questions.correctAnswer: Maintaining integrity by not allowing harmful words to influence the people
questions.explanation: Eliakim and others asked Rabshakeh not to speak in the Jewish language to protect the people's morale and integrity (Isaiah 36:11).

questions.question: What does the confrontation in Isaiah 36 teach about facing fear and intimidation with faith?
options: Faith in God's deliverance should not be shaken by enemy threats
Fear is the only reasonable response
Negotiation with enemies is always the best option
Ignoring threats leads to defeat
questions.correctAnswer: Faith in God's deliverance should not be shaken by enemy threats
questions.explanation: Despite Rabshakeh's threats, the biblical context encourages trust in God rather than fear of enemy intimidation (Isaiah 36:15).

questions.question: What does Rabshakeh's claim that the LORD told him to destroy the land imply about his understanding of God's will?
options: He believes God supports Assyria's conquest
He denies God's existence
He thinks God supports Judah only
He wants to make peace with God
questions.correctAnswer: He believes God supports Assyria's conquest
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh claims divine authorization for his actions to justify the Assyrian invasion (Isaiah 36:10).

questions.question: What practical advice can Christians learn from the officials' request to Rabshakeh to speak in a language not understood by the people?
options: Protecting the vulnerable from harmful words can preserve faith and courage
Always confront enemies in public
Avoid listening to any criticism
Speak only in foreign languages
questions.correctAnswer: Protecting the vulnerable from harmful words can preserve faith and courage
questions.explanation: The officials sought to shield the people from discouragement by limiting exposure to enemy taunts (Isaiah 36:11).

questions.question: How does Rabshakeh's speech challenge the people's trust in God and their king?
options: By asserting that neither Hezekiah nor the LORD can deliver them
By encouraging them to pray more
By warning them of God's anger
By praising Hezekiah's leadership
questions.correctAnswer: By asserting that neither Hezekiah nor the LORD can deliver them
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh tries to undermine faith by declaring that Hezekiah and the LORD will not save the city (Isaiah 36:14-15).

questions.question: What lesson does the comparison of Egypt to a 'broken reed' teach about misplaced trust?
options: That trusting unreliable allies can bring harm instead of help
That all allies are trustworthy
That Egypt is a strong protector
That broken reeds are useful
questions.correctAnswer: That trusting unreliable allies can bring harm instead of help
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh's metaphor warns against relying on Egypt, which will fail and cause injury (Isaiah 36:9).

questions.question: True or False: Rabshakeh spoke loudly in the Jewish language so that the people on the wall could understand his message.
options: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh intentionally spoke loudly in the Jewish language to reach the people on the wall (Isaiah 36:13).

hard.title: Isaiah Chapter 36 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Isaiah Chapter 36.

questions.question: According to Isaiah 36:17, to what kind of land does the king of Assyria threaten to take the people away?
options: A land like your own land, a land of corn and wine, a land of bread and vineyards
A barren and desolate land
A land of mountains and rivers
A land of darkness and despair
questions.correctAnswer: A land like your own land, a land of corn and wine, a land of bread and vineyards
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:17 explicitly states the king of Assyria's threat to take people to a land like their own, described as a land of corn, wine, bread, and vineyards.

questions.question: In Isaiah 36:18, what warning does the king of Assyria give regarding Hezekiah's message that the LORD will deliver Jerusalem?
options: Beware lest Hezekiah persuade you, saying, The LORD will deliver us
Trust in the LORD and He will protect you
Hezekiah is a prophet sent by God
Ignore all foreign threats and remain faithful
questions.correctAnswer: Beware lest Hezekiah persuade you, saying, The LORD will deliver us
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:18 includes the king of Assyria's warning to beware of Hezekiah's claim that the LORD will deliver them, challenging the efficacy of their God.

questions.question: Which gods does the king of Assyria mention in Isaiah 36:19 as examples of gods who failed to deliver their lands?
options: The gods of Hamath and Arphad, and the gods of Sepharvaim
The gods of Egypt and Babylon
The gods of Jerusalem and Judah
The gods of Assyria and Nineveh
questions.correctAnswer: The gods of Hamath and Arphad, and the gods of Sepharvaim
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:19 mentions these specific gods to mock the idea that any god has delivered their land from Assyria, illustrating his challenge to the God of Judah.

questions.question: What rhetorical question does the king of Assyria ask in Isaiah 36:20 to emphasize the futility of trusting in the LORD for deliverance?
options: Who are they among all the gods of these lands that have delivered their land out of my hand?
Why do you trust in a broken reed?
Where is your faith in your own strength?
How long will your city stand against me?
questions.correctAnswer: Who are they among all the gods of these lands that have delivered their land out of my hand?
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:20 uses this rhetorical question to assert that no gods of conquered lands have delivered them from Assyria, questioning why Jerusalem should expect different.

questions.question: According to Isaiah 36:21, what was the response of Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah to the king of Assyria's words?
options: They held their peace and answered him not a word
They responded with defiance and rebuke
They pleaded for mercy and surrender
They called upon the LORD to strike him down
questions.correctAnswer: They held their peace and answered him not a word
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:21 states that they remained silent and did not respond because of the king's commandment to answer him not.

questions.question: Who came to Hezekiah with their clothes rent to report the words of Rabshakeh as described in Isaiah 36:22?
options: Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph
Rabshakeh alone
The priests of Jerusalem
The elders of Judah and the people
questions.correctAnswer: Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:22 describes these three officials coming to Hezekiah with their clothes rent, indicating mourning and urgency, to tell him Rabshakeh's words.

questions.question: What does the Hebrew word 'Rabshakeh' (Isaiah 36:2) mean?
options: Chief officer or chief cupbearer
Messenger of peace
King's scribe
Prophet of Assyria
questions.correctAnswer: Chief officer or chief cupbearer
questions.explanation: The word 'Rabshakeh' in Isaiah 36:2 is a title meaning 'chief officer' or 'chief cupbearer,' a high-ranking Assyrian official, consistent with the context of Rabshakeh as the king's representative.

questions.question: Which literary device is evident in the repeated challenge to the gods of other nations in Isaiah 36:18-20?
options: Rhetorical questions
Simile
Metaphor
Alliteration
questions.correctAnswer: Rhetorical questions
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:18-20 employs rhetorical questions to challenge the effectiveness of other gods, reinforcing the Assyrian king's taunt against Judah's faith.

questions.question: Which New Testament passage echoes the theme of God's deliverance against overwhelming enemies as challenged in Isaiah 36:18-20?
options: Romans 8:31
Matthew 28:19
John 3:16
Revelation 21:1
questions.correctAnswer: Romans 8:31
questions.explanation: Romans 8:31 ('If God is for us, who can be against us?') echoes the theme of divine deliverance and protection despite powerful opposition, relating to the challenge in Isaiah 36:18-20.

questions.question: Which Old Testament passage fulfills the theme of trust in the LORD despite Assyrian threats as presented in Isaiah 36:14-15?
options: Genesis 12:1-3
Psalm 23
Exodus 14:21-22
questions.explanation: 2 Kings 19:32-34 recounts God's promise to protect Jerusalem from the Assyrians, fulfilling the trust in the LORD that Isaiah 36:14-15 emphasizes.

questions.question: What event immediately precedes the king of Assyria sending Rabshakeh to Jerusalem according to Isaiah 36:1-2?
options: Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah and took them
Hezekiah prayed for deliverance
The people of Jerusalem prepared for siege
The prophet Isaiah delivered a message
questions.correctAnswer: Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah and took them
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:1 states that after Sennacherib took the fortified cities of Judah, he sent Rabshakeh to Jerusalem, showing the sequence of events.

questions.question: What is the significance of Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah tearing their clothes as described in Isaiah 36:22?
options: It signifies grief and distress over Rabshakeh's threatening message
It signifies celebration of God's protection
It is a ritual cleansing before prayer
It marks a royal coronation ceremony
questions.correctAnswer: It signifies grief and distress over Rabshakeh's threatening message
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:22 describes the officials with their clothes rent, a traditional expression of mourning and distress upon hearing Rabshakeh's words.

questions.question: How does Isaiah 36:6 employ metaphorical language regarding reliance on Egypt?
options: It compares Egypt to a broken reed that pierces the hand when leaned upon
It describes Egypt as a fortress of strength
It likens Egypt to a mighty lion protecting allies
It calls Egypt a flowing river of blessings
questions.correctAnswer: It compares Egypt to a broken reed that pierces the hand when leaned upon
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:6 uses the metaphor of a 'broken reed' to illustrate the futility and danger of relying on Egypt for support against Assyria.

questions.question: What typological role does Rabshakeh’s speech in Isaiah 36:13-16 serve in the narrative of Judah’s deliverance?
options: A foreshadowing of spiritual testing and reliance on God
A direct prophecy of Jerusalem’s destruction
A figurative description of the Messiah's coming
A symbolic cleansing of the temple
questions.correctAnswer: A foreshadowing of spiritual testing and reliance on God
questions.explanation: Rabshakeh’s speech, with its threats and mockery, foreshadows the spiritual trial Judah faces, emphasizing the need for faith and reliance on God as seen in Isaiah 36:13-16.

questions.question: True or False: According to Isaiah 36:21, the king's commandment was for the officials to answer Rabshakeh's provocations with silence.
options: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:21 states that the officials held their peace and answered not a word because the king commanded them not to respond.

theological.title: Isaiah Chapter 36 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Isaiah Chapter 36 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Isaiah 36:6 teach about human trust and its consequences?
options: Trust in human allies can lead to greater harm and failure
Trusting God guarantees immediate worldly victory
All human alliances are inherently sinful and forbidden
Trusting in military strength alone is sufficient for deliverance
questions.correctAnswer: Trust in human allies can lead to greater harm and failure
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:6 uses the metaphor of a broken reed in Egypt that pierces the hand of one who leans on it, illustrating the danger and futility of trusting in human allies rather than God.

questions.question: What doctrine concerning idolatry and true worship is implied in Isaiah 36:7?
options: Removing altars to other gods is part of restoring true worship in Israel
God tolerates worship at any altar as long as prayers are sincere
The LORD’s presence is limited to specific altars and high places
Worship is unnecessary for divine protection
questions.correctAnswer: Removing altars to other gods is part of restoring true worship in Israel
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:7 highlights Hezekiah’s reforms removing high places and altars to false gods, emphasizing the doctrine that true worship is centralized and exclusive to Yahweh.

questions.question: What doctrine about divine sovereignty and human rebellion is taught in Isaiah 36:10?
options: God sovereignly uses even foreign kings to accomplish His purposes
Human rebellion can thwart God’s plans
God is limited in power and must negotiate with kings
Human kings act independently without divine permission
questions.correctAnswer: God sovereignly uses even foreign kings to accomplish His purposes
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:10 states that the LORD commanded Sennacherib to come up against the land, teaching that God is sovereign over all rulers, even those who oppose Him.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Isaiah 36:10 specifically demonstrate?
options: Sovereignty
Immanence
Omniscience
Justice
questions.correctAnswer: Sovereignty
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:10 demonstrates God’s sovereignty over nations and kings by showing that Sennacherib acts according to the LORD’s command.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is most clearly demonstrated in Isaiah 36:7 regarding Hezekiah’s religious reforms?
options: Holiness
Mercy
Omnipotence
Eternity
questions.correctAnswer: Holiness
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:7 shows God’s holiness in demanding exclusive worship and the removal of idolatrous altars.

questions.question: How does Isaiah 36:4–20 connect with the broader biblical theme of God's judgment on idolatry and trust in worldly powers?
options: It typifies God's judgment against trusting political alliances over Him
It encourages syncretism with foreign gods
It denies God's involvement in political affairs
It teaches that military power is the ultimate source of security
questions.correctAnswer: It typifies God's judgment against trusting political alliances over Him
questions.explanation: The passage shows Assyria’s king mocking Judah’s trust in Egypt and God, connecting to the recurring biblical theme that reliance on idols or foreign powers incurs divine judgment.

questions.question: What redemptive-historical connection is made by Isaiah 36:22 in reporting the distress of Hezekiah’s officials?
options: It foreshadows the faithful remnant’s perseverance despite external threats
It predicts the permanent exile of Judah without hope
It illustrates the futility of prayer in times of crisis
It anticipates the destruction of Jerusalem without divine intervention
questions.correctAnswer: It foreshadows the faithful remnant’s perseverance despite external threats
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:22 reflects the tension and distress preceding deliverance, prefiguring the faithful remnant’s endurance in redemptive history.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Isaiah 36:6 and Isaiah 36:18 teach about human trust and divine deliverance?
options: Trusting human powers is futile; only God can deliver
Egypt is a reliable ally for God’s people
Divine deliverance is guaranteed by human military strength
God’s deliverance depends on political treaties
questions.correctAnswer: Trusting human powers is futile; only God can deliver
questions.explanation: Verses 6 and 18 both emphasize the futility of relying on foreign powers like Egypt instead of trusting the LORD for deliverance.

questions.question: What combined doctrinal insight about idolatry and divine judgment is taught in Isaiah 36:7 and Isaiah 36:19?
options: False gods offer no deliverance and provoke God’s judgment
Foreign gods are equally powerful as the LORD
Judgment is reserved only for Israel, not other nations
Idolatry is a private matter without national consequences
questions.correctAnswer: False gods offer no deliverance and provoke God’s judgment
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:7 notes removal of altars to false gods, and 36:19 mocks the failure of other nations’ gods to save, teaching that idolatry leads to judgment and no true deliverance.

questions.question: What theological synthesis about divine sovereignty and human agency is drawn from Isaiah 36:10 and Isaiah 36:22?
options: God sovereignly permits threats, yet human leaders respond with faithful lament and action
Human leaders fully control historical outcomes independent of God
Divine sovereignty means human response is irrelevant
God prevents all human suffering without exception
questions.correctAnswer: God sovereignly permits threats, yet human leaders respond with faithful lament and action
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:10 shows God’s sovereignty over Assyria’s attack, and 36:22 shows Hezekiah’s officials responding with mourning and report, illustrating human responsibility under divine sovereignty.

questions.question: Skeptics claim Isaiah 36:4-20 teaches that God endorses Assyrian aggression. What does the passage actually teach?
options: God uses Assyria as an instrument of judgment, not approving its sin
God is powerless against Assyria and abandons Judah
Assyria acts independently without any divine purpose
God promotes Assyrian idolatry as a model
questions.correctAnswer: God uses Assyria as an instrument of judgment, not approving its sin
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:10 confirms God’s command to Assyria to act against Judah, showing divine sovereignty over the event, but this does not mean God endorses Assyria’s sin; rather, He uses them for judgment.

questions.question: What doctrine does Isaiah 36:1 teach about God’s providential timing in history?
options: God ordains historical events to fulfill His purposes at appointed times
Historical events are random and lack divine purpose
God intervenes only in spiritual matters, not political
God’s timing is unknowable and irrelevant
questions.correctAnswer: God ordains historical events to fulfill His purposes at appointed times
questions.explanation: The verse situates the Assyrian invasion in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, which implies God’s providential ordering of history to accomplish His plans.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is especially evident in Isaiah 36:21 in the silence of the officials?
options: Obedience
Wrath
Patience
Justice
questions.correctAnswer: Obedience
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:21 records the officials’ silence in obedience to the king’s command, indicating faithful submission to authority even in crisis.

questions.question: What theological lesson about divine judgment and human pride can be synthesized from Isaiah 36:5 and Isaiah 36:20?
options: Human pride in strength provokes divine judgment, and no false god can deliver from God’s hand
Human strength is the ultimate source of deliverance
False gods have power equal to the LORD
Human rebellion is always rewarded
questions.correctAnswer: Human pride in strength provokes divine judgment, and no false god can deliver from God’s hand
questions.explanation: Verse 5 shows arrogant speech of Assyria claiming strength, and verse 20 mocks other gods’ inability to save, teaching God’s judgment on pride and idolatry.

questions.question: How does Isaiah 36:8 reveal God’s provision in the context of human testing?
options: God permits human offers but does not guarantee success through them
God demands no human effort or provision
Military resources are divine gifts guaranteeing victory
Human attempts to negotiate with enemies are always futile
questions.correctAnswer: God permits human offers but does not guarantee success through them
questions.explanation: Isaiah 36:8 reflects Assyria’s offer of horses to intimidate, showing that human resources are permitted but ultimately under God’s sovereign control.
